sources.title: How Ross Jenkins built a $2M freelance email agency: personality, niching, and pricing by demand
sources.originalTitle: Ross Jenkins Freelance Fortune: Scaling Success to 2 Million Dollars | Denise Griffitts - Your...
sources.summary: Ross Jenkins, an Upwork top earner turned agency founder, explains why personal, story-led email still sells and why past clients are an overlooked gold mine. He also covers niching into a specialism, raising rates as demand grows, and turning away clients who haggle on price.

principles.text: Make emails read like they come from a real person; personality is what sells and email is not dead.
principles.quote: no one wants to reply to a robot um or a no reply email address or you know personality sells and that's what that's what people forget

principles.text: Email your past client list. It is the simplest, most overlooked revenue lever, and people are just scared to hit send.
principles.quote: if you email your past Client List and you've got a sale on or you've got you know you want to update them about news it's honestly a gold mine most companies miss it out

principles.text: Give people a concrete reason to opt in to your list instead of a generic 'join my newsletter' ask.
principles.quote: you want to give them a reason to opt in and normally people would be like that's a no-brainer I'm going to click it

principles.text: Niche down to one specialism; generalists get generalist pay, and buyers hire specialists for each part of a job.
principles.quote: it's about niching down and that's why why I you know I specialize in email marketing you know that's our main bread and butter

principles.text: Raise your price as demand for your time grows, and don't accept rates below your average, since low-ball buyers signal how they'll behave.
principles.quote: when we see huge sort of uproars in demand in terms of my time we know it's time to increase the the hourly rate

principles.text: Hold yourself and hires to delivering at least double the value you are paid, and know your ROI so you can price with confidence.
principles.quote: I want you to be able to add at least double the value that I'm paying you so if I'm paying you $100 an hour I want you to be able to make me $200 an hour

sources.title: Ross Jenkins on email, SMS and WhatsApp marketing, freelancing on Upwork, and avoiding common marketing mistakes
sources.summary: Ross Jenkins, CEO of DigitalME, explains how his agency uses email, SMS and WhatsApp marketing, how he built his business through Upwork, and how identity-resolution retargeting works for e-commerce. He also shares his pricing approach and the top mistakes he sees business owners make.

principles.text: Stick to the channels you can deliver best results in, rather than offering every marketing service.
principles.quote: I want to kind of stick to stick to what works and stick to what we can build like the best performance

principles.text: Drop service lines where you can't be the best, even if they were once part of your business.
principles.quote: we're amazing the emails we get great results so what's the point in being in another space that we're not going to be the best at

principles.text: Always add upsells to your site and sales flow; it's one of the biggest, most overlooked marketing wins, especially in B2C.
principles.quote: upselling probably the second biggest thing you know why haven't you got upselling on your website I don't understand especially in your BTC it makes complete sense

principles.text: Know your audience in detail and build a persona, then test different ways to reach it rather than trusting generic marketer advice.
principles.quote: understand every part of your audience and what they're doing um and build it build a Persona and then Market to it

principles.text: Price fixed-scope projects at roughly 20% over your hourly estimate to cover slow payers and scope leeway.
principles.quote: I quote 20% over what I believe it will be in terms of my hourly and then just do it that way

principles.text: Make buying as easy as possible for the customer, since people pay a premium for convenience.
principles.quote: you want to make it as easy as possible for a client to purchase

sources.title: Ross Jenkins on performance marketing, client red flags and freelancing
sources.originalTitle: You Must Understand This To Become Top & High Paid Freelancer - Ross Jenkins | 91
sources.summary: Ross Jenkins explains performance marketing as trackable, attributable spend, shows how case studies landed a dream client (UFC), and argues freelancers should fire abusive clients fast and price on value. He also makes the case that hiring a freelancer beats a full-time employee on cost.

principles.text: Performance marketing beats brand spend because every dollar is tracked back to sales and sources.
principles.quote: it's marketing that shows it's got attributions it shows where the sources are coming from and it's not just hey give me $50 million and I'll hope that you know you might actually see some sales

principles.text: Land dream clients with past-result case studies, even for a small test slice of their business.
principles.quote: the reason we we're able to do that is because we were able to show past results in terms of case studies

principles.text: Mine your existing customer list first: emailing past clients is trackable and often returns far more than the spend.
principles.quote: I'm going to be able to see every single person who spent with you every single who's clicked with you I'm going to be able to give you that data

principles.text: Define client red flags up front and cut bad clients quickly, regardless of money offered, to protect your mental health.
principles.quote: you build your own internal red flags so you can cut those people out as quickly as possible

principles.text: The ideal client doesn't haggle on price, understands your value, and doesn't demand things tomorrow.
principles.quote: the perfect claim doesn't try and negotiate on price understands how much my value is doesn't want things done tomorrow

principles.text: A freelancer is far cheaper than a full-time hire because you pay only for the hours you need, with no overhead.
principles.quote: hiring a freelance field for x amount of hours per week or a flexible basis is so much more affordable

sources.title: 5 email marketing tips to raise campaign ROI: deliverability, mobile, one CTA, segments, subject lines
sources.originalTitle: 5 Tips to Significantly Increase the ROI of Your Next Email
sources.summary: Ross Jenkins, founder of a digital agency, argues email is among the cheapest and most measurable channels, and lays out five tactical fixes. Watch deliverability first, write for mobile, use one CTA, segment the list, and use humor in subject lines to earn opens.

principles.text: Monitor deliverability first; if emails don't reach the inbox, every other metric is moot.
principles.quote: If nobody is receiving your emails, everything else is irrelevant.

principles.text: Write every email assuming it will be read on a phone: punchy subject, direct copy, responsive design.
principles.quote: When you are writing your email subject lines and copy, assume that all users are going to receive, open and view your message on a mobile device.

principles.text: Give each email one clear call to action so recipients know exactly what to do.
principles.quote: If you want to see your emails convert at a higher rate, include a single call to action, and tell your recipient what that action is and what you want them to do.

principles.text: Segment your list instead of blasting everyone; start with customers vs non-customers and split further from there.
principles.quote: If you are sending the same message to your entire email list, you are missing a huge opportunity and leaving a lot of money on the table every time you deploy a message.

principles.text: The subject line gates all return, so make it stand out and test humor and shock value.
principles.quote: Your subject line needs to command attention and trigger the recipient to click on it.

principles.text: Email is cheap, highly measurable, and can be tuned to outperform other channels, yet most businesses under-invest in it.
principles.quote: Many businesses put very little effort into their email marketing, and it shows.

sources.title: Website traffic metrics: five sub-metrics to tie traffic to revenue
sources.originalTitle: 5 Critical Website Traffic Metrics You Should Know
sources.summary: Ross Jenkins argues raw traffic volume is a vanity metric and that traffic only matters if it converts to revenue. He breaks website traffic into five sub-metrics (unique visitors, bounce rate, referral sources, CPV/RPV, and page views/duration) so you can scale the best sources and cut the worst.

principles.text: Revenue is the goal; traffic that doesn't convert to revenue is worthless, and visit counts alone mean nothing.
principles.quote: The name of the game is revenue. If your website traffic isn’t converting into revenue, it’s essentially worthless.

principles.text: Break traffic into sub-metrics, then scale the best sources and pull back the weakest.
principles.quote: When you know where your most valuable traffic originates from, you can increase those efforts, and when you know what your lowest performing traffic source, is you can pull back those efforts.

principles.text: Count unique visitors, not raw visits, and watch the trend over time to spot a source drying up.
principles.quote: If a traffic source continues to drop in terms of unique visitors, it signals that it might be drying up and becoming less effective at introducing new people to your business.

principles.text: A high bounce rate signals a mismatch between the offer and the page; use heat maps to find the disconnect.
principles.quote: If you have a high bounce rate, you might want to install a heat-map tool on your website to see where your visitors are clicking and how far they are scrolling.

principles.text: Reverse engineer each referral source by revenue and cost per conversion, then scale the cheaper one.
principles.quote: If one traffic source is bringing you sales at a $15 conversion cost, but another one is delivering the same traffic value at $8 per conversion, wouldn’t it make sense to scale the lower cost referral source?

principles.text: Track cost-per-visitor and revenue-per-visitor for every traffic source to budget and plan growth.
principles.quote: You should know these numbers for every traffic source you use.

sources.title: How to choose a website platform: match the tool to your use, skills and budget
sources.originalTitle: 5 Things to Consider When Selecting a Website Platform
sources.summary: Ross Jenkins, founder of digital agency DigitalME, argues there is no best website platform, only the one that fits your goals. He walks through five filters: intended use, technical expertise, budget, design customization, and ease of updating. Cheap, mainstream platforms like Shopify and WordPress can carry very large businesses.

principles.text: Pick a platform based on what the site must do, not on generic 'best platform' lists.
principles.quote: Before you blindly select a website platform, there are some things you need to consider to find the best website platform for your specific needs

principles.text: Avoid both under-built and over-built sites; match platform to actual need.
principles.quote: Far too many times, businesses will be on a platform that isn’t up to par in terms of what they need or they build on something that is complete overkill.

principles.text: A website is a growth tool; invest in learning it, or it won't drive sales.
principles.quote: a Shopify store that connects a domain, uploads some products, and then lets it sit there isn’t going to grow quickly, if at all.

principles.text: Technical skill unlocks tracking, abandonment recovery and upselling that lift sales.
principles.quote: someone with a lot of technical knowledge can leverage the tracking and insights to drive more sales and then utilize abandonment recovery and upselling

principles.text: Low-cost platforms scale: don't dismiss them as unfit for big companies.
principles.quote: Some of the largest ecommerce brands in the world run on Shopify and generate millions of dollars daily using the same tech stack that is available to you.

principles.text: Without a dev team, choose a platform with strong learning resources you can follow yourself.
principles.quote: look for a platform that you feel comfortable (and confident) learning about. Today, almost anything related to development can be found on YouTube.

sources.title: Driving traffic from LinkedIn to your website: 7 tactics
sources.originalTitle: 7 Ways to Drive Traffic From LinkedIn to Your Website
sources.summary: Ross Jenkins, founder of digital agency DigitalME, lays out seven basic LinkedIn tactics for sending traffic to a website: a credible profile, a large first-degree network, groups, steady posting, curiosity-driven link titles, and an RSS blog feed. The advice is generic and tactical, with no data from his own results.

principles.text: A clean, organized, professional profile makes you more credible to a target audience, and credibility drives clicks to your site.
principles.quote: the more organized and professional a profile is, the more credible it appears to a target audience.

principles.text: Build a large first-degree network (start at 500+) to widen reach and the number of people who see your website link.
principles.quote: The goal should be to start with at least 500 first-degree connections, then continue building from there by personalizing connection requests

principles.text: Join relevant groups to find like-minded people and post content that pulls target audiences to your site.
principles.quote: you can also post your content there to entice target audiences to visit your site and so gain access to more content.

principles.text: Create your own group to position yourself as an expert and amplify reach, but commit to engaging the audience constantly.
principles.quote: managing your own LinkedIn group comes with responsibilities, such as constantly engaging with an audience.

principles.text: Post a steady stream of engaging content about daily, but avoid oversharing or spamming, which backfires.
principles.quote: Sharing new content (perhaps including images, videos and other striking elements) at least once a day can effectively keep an audience’s attention

principles.text: Write link titles that spark curiosity and summarize what the reader gets, instead of generic labels like 'My Blog'.
principles.quote: Titles should be simple and concise, appeal to what a target audience is looking for, and should effectively summarize what they will get by clicking.

sources.title: Ross Jenkins on Starting Your Marketing: A Checklist of Basic Channels
sources.originalTitle: 7 Ways to Market Your Business for Maximum Profit
sources.summary: A generic beginner checklist for small-business marketing: plan first, build a website, show up on social media, claim your online listings, run a few targeted ads, network locally, use coupons and free trials, and stay consistent. Broad and light on specifics, but a usable starting list.

principles.text: Great products aren't enough; strong marketing sets you apart and can carry even mediocre products.
principles.quote: it is not enough to simply have high-quality products and services. You also need to have a strong marketing game so that you can set yourself apart from your competitors

principles.text: Start with a simple plan tied to ROI, plus a 30-second pitch tested on people in advance.
principles.quote: You do not have to make your plan big. What is important is that it is beneficial for your ROI.

principles.text: Control what people find when they search for you by claiming your business listings.
principles.quote: You would want to see and control what people read about your products or services when they search for you.

principles.text: In paid search, pick a few quality keywords rather than many, and use location and budget controls.
principles.quote: Rather than picking out a lot of keywords, it is best to choose a few quality keywords.

principles.text: Free trials and coupons start building followers, since satisfied customers return and share their experience.
principles.quote: A customer who is satisfied with what you have to offer will return and share his or her experience with his or her family and friends.

principles.text: Be consistent; people can't buy from a business they don't know exists.
principles.quote: you have to be consistent. You have to make sure that your business is known.

sources.title: Why buy a turnkey business: skipping research, setup and customer acquisition
sources.originalTitle: 9 Compelling Reasons to Buy a Turnkey Business
sources.summary: Ross Jenkins argues that buying an existing turnkey business beats starting from scratch because you inherit market research, a proven model, a loyal customer base and seller support. It is a generic, listicle-style case for acquisition over startup, with a closing reminder to do due diligence and consult experts before signing.

principles.text: Buying an existing business lets you reuse prior market research and inventory data instead of researching from zero.
principles.quote: Since it is not new to the market and has been at the same location for a while, you have insight into the customers.

principles.text: A proven, replicable model removes guesswork about strategy and profit maximization for new owners.
principles.quote: Turnkey businesses offer a setup that eliminates the guesswork common with new entrepreneurs who are unsure of which strategy to use to maximize profit.

principles.text: Winning customers from competitors is the hardest part of business and often costs heavy discounts; an established base avoids that.
principles.quote: The hardest part about running a business is getting people to switch from a competitor’s product to yours.

principles.text: Existing customers cut the marketing spend and promotional offers a from-scratch startup needs to attract buyers.
principles.quote: Starting a business from scratch entails a lot of marketing costs and offers to attract new customers.

principles.text: Seller support (tech, marketing, training, operations) raises your odds of success after a purchase.
principles.quote: By partnering with a supportive business franchisor, you have better chances of driving your business in the right direction and increasing your chances of success.

principles.text: Do thorough due diligence before buying: research, talk to current owners, and consult experts.
principles.quote: before settling for any turnkey business you come across, remember to conduct thorough research and schedule a consultation with the current business owners before signing a contract.

sources.title: How to hire freelancers for a remote team: referrals, clear listings, qualifiers, hire slow fire fast
sources.originalTitle: How to Hire the Best Freelancers When Building a Remote Team
sources.summary: Ross Jenkins, founder of a digital agency, gives a practical checklist for hiring remote freelancers. It covers sourcing through referrals and multiple marketplaces, writing precise job listings, screening with a simple qualifier, video calls, references and test tasks, and moving fast to remove bad hires.

principles.text: Start talent sourcing with referrals from fellow entrepreneurs in your circle.
principles.quote: Firing off a few emails and text messages to your circle of entrepreneurial friends is a great starting point.

principles.text: Post on several freelance marketplaces, not just one, to widen the talent pool.
principles.quote: Never limit your search to just one freelance marketplace, as many talented candidates don’t register for all of them.

principles.text: Spell out requirements and qualifications precisely to attract better applicants and cut unqualified ones.
principles.quote: The more clear you are about what you are hiring for, what you expect, what the qualifications are, and what the job description is, the better qualified your applicants will be.

principles.text: Add a simple qualifier to the application; anyone who can't follow it is not detail-oriented.
principles.quote: If they cannot follow a simple instruction, delete them, as they are not attentive to details.

principles.text: Verify candidates with video calls, reference checks and real test assignments, since paper credentials aren't enough.
principles.quote: Anyone can look good on paper. You often need to see how he or she works in the real world and with your team to truly evaluate his or her potential.

principles.text: Hire slow and fire fast: take your time choosing, and remove a bad hire quickly because the damage compounds.
principles.quote: The longer you keep someone around that is bad for your company, the more damage he or she will do.

sources.title: UFC vs boxing marketing: promote personas, not events, and control the distribution
sources.originalTitle: What to Learn From UFC's and Boxing's Marketing Strategies
sources.summary: Ross Jenkins compares UFC's centralized, fighter-persona-driven, digital-first model with boxing's fragmented promoter model and print/PPV reach. He draws marketing and business lessons on brand control, storytelling, fair pay for brand reputation, and using digital channels for younger audiences.

principles.text: Promote the people and their stories, not just the events; personas draw audiences in.
principles.quote: Instead of focusing on the events themselves, UFC tends to promote the fighters by building up their personas and their stories. It’s an effective tool that can draw more people in.

principles.text: Owning the whole value chain gives you control and higher margins, but can strain the people you rely on.
principles.quote: Looking at the operating side, UFC as a whole earns more since everything is produced in-house. However, the same can’t be said of their fighters.

principles.text: Match channel to audience: traditional audiences respond to print and live, younger adults to digital.
principles.quote: Boxing is concentrated on folks who are more traditional; that’s why they focus their promoting strategies using traditional marketing. On the other hand, UFC garners more viewership from younger adults.

principles.text: Ethical treatment of partners is a brand asset; buyers drop products with questionable sourcing.
principles.quote: If a product they like wasn’t sourced ethically, then they’ll drop it even if they like it.

principles.text: Don't restrict partners' outside deals; blocking sponsorships can cost you ad-revenue opportunities.
principles.quote: They should also be allowed more sponsorships and deals. Restricting these can end up costing them fewer opportunities from ad revenues.

principles.text: Even a solid strategy should fully use social and digital marketing tools to leverage growth.
principles.quote: Utilizing every aspect of digital marketing will help UFC leverage the sport.

sources.title: Marketing lessons from Jake Paul: brand, audience appreciation and sponsorships
sources.originalTitle: Why Businesses Should Take a Page Out of Jake Paul's Book
sources.summary: Ross Jenkins uses Jake Paul as a case study for businesses. Key takeaways: appreciate your customers, build a recognizable brand, set high targets, believe in your offer, and use sponsorships (financial or in-kind) to borrow an influencer's audience. It is a high-level listicle with little concrete data.

principles.text: Appreciate your customers and give them news first; your business exists because of them.
principles.quote: Always appreciate them; show your clients that you’ve made it so far in business because of them.

principles.text: Build a personal or business brand boldly; being noticed drives growth and sales.
principles.quote: Don’t be afraid to build up your name. It helps a lot in growth and sales.

principles.text: Differentiate by doing business differently and finding new ways to market your brand.
principles.quote: He built his brand by doing business differently, embracing the controversies that make him more famous.

principles.text: Set high targets and believe your offer is the best in the market.
principles.quote: You have to believe that whatever you are offering is the best in the market at that current time.

principles.text: Sponsorships (financial or in-kind) let brands borrow an influencer's audience for awareness and credibility.
principles.quote: by using the large following of a social-media influencer like him, they can increase their brand awareness and credibility.

principles.text: Choosing the right sponsors for your content improves your odds of online success.
principles.quote: finding the right sponsors for your content can increase your chances for success.

sources.title: Freelance time management: visualize goals, prioritize, schedule, cut distractions, say no
sources.originalTitle: 5 Tips to Properly Manage Your Time as a Freelancer
sources.summary: Ross Jenkins, founder of DigitalME, gives five practical time management habits for freelancers. He covers goal visualization, ranking work by value and urgency, logging tasks on a calendar, removing distractions, and refusing work to avoid burnout. The advice is generic but reflects a stability-over-volume mindset.

principles.text: Keep your goal visible daily so your time decisions orient toward it.
principles.quote: Reading the same message with your main goal every morning will make your time management oriented towards achieving it.

principles.text: Rank work by value or urgency; do critical tasks first and archive the rest.
principles.quote: Activities that aren’t important or urgent can be deleted or archived indefinitely until all others have been completed.

principles.text: Log every task with details, deadlines and status on a calendar to measure productivity.
principles.quote: Keeping a log of your tasks will help you measure your productivity.

principles.text: Remove distractions by using a dedicated workspace and blocking social media during work hours.
principles.quote: it’s a good practice to choose a workplace exclusively for your freelance activities so that it is impossible for you to try to do something different.

principles.text: Overloading yourself with jobs causes missed deadlines and damages client relationships.
principles.quote: It’s essential to keep yourself mentally healthy by only taking the jobs you can handle.

principles.text: Aim for stable long-term work rather than grabbing every job, and learn to say no.
principles.quote: A necessary skill to succeed in freelancing is the ability to reject jobs when you know you don’t have the time to do them.

sources.title: Freelancing: 6 steps to attract clients and win repeat work
sources.originalTitle: 6 Steps to Becoming a Successful Freelancer
sources.summary: A practical checklist for new freelancers on getting hired. It covers listing on platforms, tapping personal networks, narrowing your niche, staying responsive, earning repeat work, and bringing in collaborators honestly.

principles.text: Platform traffic helps, but how you sell yourself decides whether you get hired.
principles.quote: Although the website traffic matters in terms of you getting hired, in the end, it all boils down to how you “sell” yourself to employers.

principles.text: Don't rely on platforms alone; tell your personal circle, whose referrals carry built-in trust.
principles.quote: Connect with your social circles and make your services known to those whom you know personally.

principles.text: Sell a specific niche, not a vague skill label, because clients hire for specific jobs.
principles.quote: Instead of generalizing your skills, try to sell within your niche specifically.

principles.text: Be proactive: apply to gigs yourself and price a bit below peers, but not so low it signals poor work.
principles.quote: Make it reasonable, yet lower than most freelancers.

principles.text: Respond fast and update often to build client confidence and ensure on-time delivery.
principles.quote: Furthermore, remember to be as responsive as possible — answer whatever queries clients have as soon as you receive them and always be professional and polite.

principles.text: Exceed expectations, then pitch follow-on projects; impressed clients trust you with more work.
principles.quote: If they’re thoroughly impressed with your previous work, then the chances of them trusting you on the work that follows are high.

sources.title: Why digital tools help small businesses cut costs, communicate, market and expand
sources.originalTitle: How the Right Digital Tools Can Help Your Business Win
sources.summary: A 2021 Entrepreneur op-ed arguing that founders should invest early in digital tools. Covers cloud tools to cut overhead, communication and task-management software, brand-building apps, and analytics, SEO and CRM tools for lead generation. General and tool-focused, with few concrete numbers or tactics.

principles.text: Don't skip digital tools to save money early; adopting them now creates more room for integration and growth later.
principles.quote: By adopting the latest technologies today, you will have more chances for integration, development and prosperity in the future.

principles.text: Use cloud tools to cut operating costs, such as running remote with no office space or utility bills.
principles.quote: Cloud storage and computing technologies can let you run your business without the need for office space, resulting in zero utility expenses.

principles.text: Pick project-management software based on the specific tasks you need help with, such as collaboration for remote teams.
principles.quote: When deciding which software to purchase, given that most of them are paid, you have to consider the tasks you need help with.

principles.text: Brand awareness drives growth; build it with visual marketing tools and social-media management tools.
principles.quote: How can you expect to grow your client base and revenues if your target audience is unfamiliar with your brand?

principles.text: Use analytics, SEO and CRM software to track traffic, see competitors' rankings and expand your customer base.
principles.quote: If you want to track site traffic, internal links and the regions from which people access your site, Google Analytics is a must-have tool.

principles.text: Define your goal first, then research the best-fit tools; they save time and can reduce the need for extra hires.
principles.quote: All of these technologies save you time and may eliminate the need for additional workers, giving you the time and budget you need to expand.

sources.title: How to double freelance income on Upwork in a year: proposals, retainers, consultations, raises
sources.originalTitle: How to Make More Money on Upwork: Double Income in a Year
sources.summary: Ross Jenkins lays out a tactical playbook for doubling freelance income on Upwork: send more proposals, respond fast, add income streams (consultations, productized catalog projects), push for weekly retainers, target long-term clients, and raise rates yearly. The advice is marketplace-specific but the funnel and pricing logic is general.

principles.text: Treat sales as a funnel: more proposals means more interviews, more jobs, and better close rates through practice.
principles.quote: The more proposals I send, the more interviews I get. The more interviews I get, the more jobs I land.

principles.text: Volume only works if targeted: read briefs closely and spend effort only on jobs that fit your work and income goals.
principles.quote: be sure to read the job descriptions closely and make sure they align with your work and income goals.

principles.text: Respond to leads quickly. Inbound messages and invites are revenue, so check inboxes through the day and answer invites within 24 hours.
principles.quote: I periodically take a look at my invitation response statistics, too, in order to make sure that I’m responding to all invites within 24 hours.

principles.text: Diversify income streams: proposals, paid consultations, and listed productized services each bring clients in a different way.
principles.quote: Not only do I send proposals through Talent Marketplace™, I also offer paid consultations and list services for sale in Project Catalog™.

principles.text: Propose retainer-style weekly payments to smooth income, with hourly overage billing when the client needs more.
principles.quote: I’m paid this amount every week, even if the client doesn’t need me to complete five hours of work.

principles.text: Raise your rates regularly. A modest rate increase compounds revenue without adding hours.
principles.quote: That’s a 25% increase to your revenue right there, even if you didn’t increase your hours worked.

sources.title: Ross Jenkins on Upwork: 8 account-ban risks and how to protect your freelance business
sources.originalTitle: These 8 Things Could Get You Banned On Upwork
sources.summary: Ross Jenkins, founder of DigitalME, lists eight behaviors that get freelancers banned on Upwork, such as off-platform chats and billing, fake reviews, and padded hours. The practical takeaway for running a freelance or agency business is to protect your platform account, keep payment protection, and build reputation through real client work.

principles.text: Keep client chats and billing on the platform until a contract starts; it protects you from scams and gives you recourse.
principles.quote: By only chatting with prospective clients through Upwork Messages—and this includes starting a Zoom or phone call through the platform—you can get help from Upwork if you feel that someone’s attempting to run a scam or take advantage of you.

principles.text: Escrow and hourly payment protection are why on-platform billing is safer than invoicing clients directly.
principles.quote: If it’s a fixed price contract, the client pays for the first milestone in advance. Upwork holds this money in escrow for you, meaning it’s secure in an account that only Upwork can touch.

principles.text: Earn reviews by doing quality work for real clients; faking or bribing for feedback risks your account and standing.
principles.quote: The best way to get good feedback on your Upwork profile is by doing high-quality work for real clients!

principles.text: Use a team or agency openly, but never pass off work you lack rights to as your own original product.
principles.quote: You can absolutely work with a team or build an agency on Upwork.

principles.text: Represent yourself with a real name and photo; trust is what lets clients hire someone they only meet online.
principles.quote: They still want to know that they’re working with a real person they can trust.

principles.text: Be transparent with clients about how you track hours, and only log time actually worked.
principles.quote: I log my hours manually and am fully transparent beforehand with clients about how I log hours, and why I prefer the method that I use.

sources.title: Covid-era survival: automate your business by moving it online (Ross Jenkins, DigitalME)
sources.originalTitle: The Secret To Saving Your Business Amidst Covid19, Ross Jenkins at DigitalME
sources.summary: Ross Jenkins, founder of marketing agency DigitalME, argues that during Covid19 a business can either cut costs and wait or transform by automating. He uses a gym example (online sessions, a lead-magnet freebie, email list, pre-sold packages, membership site) and warns against DIY automation. Short and promotional, with one useful funnel pattern.

principles.text: In a shock, don't just cut costs and wait; push your boundaries and transform the business by automating it.
principles.quote: However, you could also push your boundaries and absolutely transform your business by automating it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ross Jenkins, an Upwork top earner turned agency founder, explains why personal, story-led email still sells and why past clients are an overlooked gold mine. He also covers niching into a specialism, raising rates as demand grows, and turning away clients who haggle on price.

chunks.heading: Freelancing as a business: Upwork pricing, rates and positioning
chunks.text:
- Ross joined Upwork in 2018 and started at $25 an hour. He now charges $365 an hour.
- His rule for raising rates: "when we see huge sort of uproars in demand in terms of my time we know it's time to increase the hourly rate."
- His first client was a pub owner in Los Angeles. Ross raised his price as demand grew until the work was no longer profitable for the pub. They parted on good terms, and the client may come back.
- He says hiring on Upwork is largely about confidence. If a freelancer isn't confident in their hourly rate, clients won't trust the work.
- He argues freelancers should build up their feedback at their real rate. A $30-an-hour freelancer who accepts a $6 job drags the visible rate on their profile back down to where they started.
- Ross says Upwork has a large share of freelancers who have never landed a job. He guesses around 80%, and flags that as a guess. Reasons he gives: no portfolio, unrealistic hourly rates (his girlfriend's brother listed at $10,000 an hour with nothing to show), and not applying to jobs.
- Upwork and Fiverr overlap, but he sees Upwork as the more upmarket marketplace. On either you can find an admin for $3 an hour or a specialist at a very high price.
- He recommends exams and certifications, both on Upwork and external ones such as HubSpot, to become "better than the people you're competing with."

chunks.heading: Specialize: niche down instead of being a generalist
chunks.text:
- Ross's own niche is email marketing and CRM. He takes other work only when it falls within the scope of what the agency does well.
- Generalist freelancers get "generalist pay" and compete with people who "scrape the barrel" on price.
- He says crowded categories such as social media marketing, admin and customer support have far more supply than demand. Some people charge $2-3 an hour.
- His advice for those categories is to upskill and build a brand, or do something distinctive. For example, customer support freelancers can build Zendesk macros or FAQs for companies instead of just answering tickets.
- He cites freelancers who earn well in these niches, such as an Upwork admin making about $200,000 a year, because they made themselves the go-to person.
- He dislikes the "marketing manager with 20 roles" pattern (account manager, SEO, content, email, admin). Nobody is good at all of those.
- Example: for a Gravity Forms job he would hire one person to build the form and another to design it, because specialists beat a generalist.
- He warns against handing specialist work to an office manager or admin, such as cleansing and emailing the client database, which he calls a "gold mine." The admin is usually untrained for it and ends up resentful.

chunks.heading: Price on value, and turn away clients who only want cheap
chunks.text:
- Ross wants freelancers to add at least double what they cost. If he pays someone $100 an hour, he wants them to generate $200 an hour for him.
- Freelancers need case studies that show this, and need to understand why they are worth their rate.
- He pushes back on "they can't afford it" thinking: you can't put yourself in the client's shoes. Focus on the value you bring and how you help them grow.
- When a prospect offers less than his rate, he tells them to go work with someone else. If they come back and ask for his rate after trying to negotiate, he still won't take them. They have already shown they want to pay as little as possible.
- He fires clients too, including one who spoke badly to freelancers in a shared Slack group and then spoke that way to Ross. His reasoning: for many freelancers a client is their livelihood, and treating them badly isn't acceptable.
- He says freelancers should value their mental health and their time. A client who demands work immediately when the freelancer has already used the booked hours is not worth keeping.
- Agency approach to pricing: "we're pretty Cutthroat" about who they take on. Past mistakes with misfit clients taught him which prospects to avoid.
- Commission deals: for founders and products he believes in, the agency will work partly or wholly on commission to give "a bit more drive." Ross says his door-to-door sales background makes this comfortable.
- He claims his team has made over $150 million for companies. As one example, a company with about 30 years in business and no email list before he started now makes about $4 million a year from email.

chunks.heading: Email marketing: personality, relevance and giving a reason to opt in
chunks.text:
- Ross says email isn't dead. He sees a "massive pickup" this year, after growth since he entered the field five years ago.
- Email works for notifications, newsletters, sales and upsell emails, for both B2B and B2C. He thinks every business should have an email system.
- People give up too early: "no one wants to reply to a robot." Personality sells.
- His emails are personalized and come from a real person. They look as authentic as two people emailing each other, not from a no-reply address.
- Be relatable to the specific audience. His example: for CEOs, relate the pitch to something like an upsell at Starbucks. For moms, build an audience in Facebook groups with relevant messaging.
- Tell a story about why the email is valuable in this person's inbox. He has had clients with 30,000 contacts on paper and no idea what message they wanted to send.
- Show value in the first lines. He criticizes cold outreach on LinkedIn that gives no reason and shows no research.
- Email your past client list. He calls it a "gold mine" most companies miss, and "one of the simplest ways to increase your revenue." People are scared to hit send, but he says it's worth it.
- He is wary of adding people to a list without asking. His agency adds buyers to the list as part of purchase and makes opting out clear. Fewer than one or two people have opted out.
- For a first email to past clients, send something personal. Give an update and a link to join the newsletter if they want more.
- Sell the newsletter itself with a concrete reason to join. Example for an Amazon seller audience: tips on improving listing SEO, pricing to compete, and better product images.
- Scarcity can work for B2C: "I can only take a hundred people on this newsletter" or "I've given all my tips and tricks for the next 100 days."
- For B2B, state why they should be on the list, and consider a discount. Make it a bold statement and be "personable," not "personal."

chunks.heading: Cold email is relationship building
chunks.text:
- Ross says cold email still works but takes time. You're building a new relationship, which is harder than emailing past clients.
- Clients who want sales "tomorrow" from a cold campaign will be disappointed. Relationships don't work that way.
- He compares the skill to driving a manual car in Europe: it takes practice, and people who try one email and quit never learn it.
- Between new audiences and existing ones, channel choice depends on age demographics. He mentions TikTok, Instagram, Facebook and X as channels that skew to different ages.

chunks.heading: Hiring and running a freelance team
chunks.text:
- Ross uses freelancers across the world and has built the agency (Digital Me) around them. The team has ranged from about 12 to about 40 freelancers as he learned what worked.
- His first contractor is still with him.
- Reasons to use freelancers over full-time hires: a US web developer might cost around $100,000 a year plus insurance and a desk. If you only have about 20 hours of work, a freelancer is better.
- Hiring locally limits you. "The best email marketer in Chicago" is not the best in the world. Hiring globally lets you find top talent anywhere. He mentions graphic designers in Ukraine and developers in India and the Philippines.
- Specialists beat generalists at the same price.
- Give experts creative freedom. Ross asks developers how they would approach something (for example a HubSpot dashboard request) rather than dictating: "I'm the expert in marketing and they're the expert in that."
- He lets people go who keep missing deadlines or who charge but don't deliver. In one example, he was chasing a developer for late work and decided "why am I chasing you, you should be chasing me to give you work."
- Late work lands on him, because he is the one who goes back to the client.

chunks.heading: Quality control and acting on emotion
chunks.text:
- Everything the agency delivers passes through two or three people, and Ross himself, who check the code or front end.
- Reason: after ten hours of work you can miss something, and a second or third reviewer catches it. This is a big part of why the agency is higher end.
- The agency won't do cheap work, for example a "$20 HTML page." Prospects who say they'll hire a cheaper developer or use Elementor are told to go ahead.
- On emotional decisions, Ross says to cool down before acting: "you don't want to make decisions based on emotions." He estimates 99% of hotheaded decisions are wrong.

chunks.heading: Tooling by building in-house, and the gig economy outlook
chunks.text:
- Ross's agency recommended a contact-cleansing tool to about 50 clients, which he says generated over $400,000 for them. He then had a developer build the same script in a few hours and wished they had done it sooner. He attributes the delay to not giving freelancers enough responsibility.
- He keeps learning from Twitter and Social Media Examiner, looking for better tools and ways to be more effective.
- Outlook: he thinks the gig economy will keep growing. He points to labor shortages and high pay for low-wage work (McDonald's at over $20 an hour in California) as signs more companies will turn to freelancers.
- He expects some return to offices after COVID to cause a "rumble," but thinks freelancing is here for good.
- Employers once held back on remote work and treated people badly, which he thinks pushed workers toward freelancing.
- His background: small-town England, eight months of door-to-door internet sales, then agency work in Ireland, Qatar and England. He left because agencies took a huge cut and had gaps in communication and quality, then went to Barcelona alone for about six months to build his own business.
- He now splits time between Spain and Dubai.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ross Jenkins, CEO of DigitalME, explains how his agency uses email, SMS and WhatsApp marketing, how he built his business through Upwork, and how identity-resolution retargeting works for e-commerce. He also shares his pricing approach and the top mistakes he sees business owners make.

chunks.heading: Ross's background and how he got into email marketing
chunks.text:
- Ross Jenkins is CEO of DigitalME (digital me.cc), a full-service agency that specializes in email marketing: setup, diagnostics, analytics and audience understanding.
- He has about 12 years in marketing. He started at a UK agency and kept working for agencies afterward.
- He learned what clients hate about agencies: "communication sucked" and agencies "take the money and then work out how you're going to deal with it." His view: "You don't sell a car and hope for the best."
- His first business was a friends-and-family investment called SMS to PayPal. PayPal was hard to fund for under-18s but accepted everywhere, and the product let them fund it by SMS. It worked well and he declined purchase offers.
- That business taught him how SMS works. He then moved to agencies and fell for the "gratification" of campaigns going out and working.
- Clients are mostly under 50 staff, plus some bigger names, including people who have run for US president.

chunks.heading: Going independent and pricing on Upwork
chunks.text:
- In Ireland he was getting strong results for agency clients. He made a verbal deal with a CEO, hit his side, and the CEO didn't. He treats that as a lesson not to rely on verbal agreements.
- He tried negotiating a percentage of agency business, then decided to go alone once agencies saw his potential.
- He wanted something like escrow, because clients don't want to send $100,000 up front.
- He joined Upwork when freelancing was small and no one had earned over $100,000.
- Starting rate: $25/hour. Current rate: $365/hour. He reports just under $2 million earned on the platform.
- He stayed exclusive to Upwork on purpose, to focus on one goal. His logic: more earnings on Upwork means more trust and more hires. He avoided Fiverr because of its low-price reputation and the one-off-gig audience.
- Upwork suits his target clients: higher-end, ongoing work of 5-10 hours a week rather than one- or two-hour gigs.
- He still keeps his Upwork profile, accepting the fees, because it works as a marketing platform. Most clients now come direct as the brand has grown.
- Fixed-price quotes: he quotes about 20% over his estimated hourly cost. That covers scope creep and slow-paying clients.

chunks.heading: Channels he sells and why he sticks to them
chunks.text:
- Core channels: email, SMS and WhatsApp.
- He avoids ads and other channels because "ads either work amazingly or it's a massive hole." He sticks to what he can build the best performance in.
- He does not do billboards or print.
- He used to offer SEO and web work but dropped them. Clients wanted the cheapest price and tools like Elementor let anyone build their own site. His reasoning: "What's the point in being in another space that we're not going to be the best at?"
- He works with outside specialists when a client needs more. For example, a Facebook ads contractor, paying for a landing page and opt-in form that feeds email on the back end. He trusts partners he has vetted and has spent tens of thousands of dollars on PPC with people he trusts.
- Stack: ActiveCampaign for email and SMS, with a custom tool built on top for WhatsApp.

chunks.heading: SMS and WhatsApp mechanics
chunks.text:
- SMS has no spam folder, so messages deliver. The risk is carriers: "phone operators are like the mafia."
- Carriers (AT&T, Verizon in the US; Vodafone and others in the UK) judge by sender reputation. A new sender has none and can't build it without sending.
- One misstep can destroy reputation. Big senders like Domino's and Papa John's have earned a reputation that lets them send weekly. He says money and connections can buy that.
- One client has 10,000 customers who spend tens of thousands of dollars each. They only SMS them three times a year because carriers make it hard.
- Opt-out is a legal requirement for SMS and email. In email, a missing unsubscribe button pushes people to hit spam.
- WhatsApp: strong in the Middle East and Europe, where people don't open email as much but "will WhatsApp you all day." The US uses it less.
- He believes WhatsApp marketing will overtake SMS in the UK and Middle East, helped by Meta releasing an API. He is unsure how long Meta will keep it open, and it has similar anti-spam rules (spam thousands of numbers and they ban you).
- He notes WhatsApp runs over data or Wi-Fi rather than a carrier plan, and sends images better than MMS.

chunks.heading: Send-time optimization
chunks.text:
- ActiveCampaign's predictive send picks each person's optimal send time.
- It doesn't just use when they open. Example: someone may open emails at 9:00 a.m. while skimming and deleting. At 11:00 a.m. at their desk they read, click and reply, and that becomes the optimal time.
- So one contact might get sends at 11:00 a.m. and another at 12:45 a.m., based on engaged behavior rather than raw opens.
- It's a fix for messages arriving at odd hours, like a 3 a.m. text.

chunks.heading: Retargeting by email with Retention
chunks.text:
- Ross describes standard retargeting ads (Google/Facebook cookies) and a second approach: a tool called Retention, US-only.
- How it works as he describes it: a visitor to a client's site is matched against legally purchased US databases. The client gets the visitor's email and can email them without the visitor submitting anything.
- Segmentation can go down to the product viewed. For example, someone who looked at a recipe gets an email about the ready meal.
- Best fit: e-commerce stores. He says the results are "insane" and his clients see strong conversions. One client with five competitor tools says Retention beats them, getting about 2,000 contacts a day and roughly $22-25K in sales from that alone.
- Cost: he says under about $1,000 a month. Justified when the site has roughly 10,000 US visitors a month, or fewer if each customer is worth a lot (example: a $50,000 customer at 5,000 visitors a month).
- DigitalME's role: send clients to Retention, help install it, and build the email flows in ActiveCampaign or another CRM.
- He expects it to survive in the US given light regulation but is unsure.

chunks.heading: Who he takes on and what he won't do
chunks.text:
- Bought lists: people come to him about every five to six weeks with a "phone book" of a million addresses from different niches that they have never spoken to. He turns them away. Mailing strangers lands you in spam and the client comes back upset.
- Minimum economics: if the product is about $5 and there are no existing customers, cost of acquisition versus margin doesn't work. His soft spot is roughly $200-300 per product or more. He's worked with clients selling $2,000-$10,000 courses.
- Enterprise example: a campaign to about 6,000 hotels worldwide for feedback on a fitness product can cost only a couple thousand dollars. Pure conversion goals cost more and take time, and his marketing budget advice "varies so hard."

chunks.heading: Top marketing mistakes he sees
chunks.text:
1. Doing it yourself badly: owners who never email their list, or send emails with a logo the full size of the screen. He has also seen CEOs cut costs wildly.
2. No upselling: "Why haven't you got upselling on your website?" Especially for B2C. He cites Temu as an aggressive upseller and says traditional sites upsell far less than they should.
3. Not knowing your audience: build a persona covering age, gender, location, job, and so on. Different audiences respond to different channels (TikTok for 18-25, Instagram/Facebook for 35-55). Test with your own data, since many marketing speakers haven't marketed in 10-15 years.

His tip on upsell: the movie theater example, where offering a larger soda for 25 cents more won yes about 80% of the time, which helps both the customer and the business.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ross Jenkins explains performance marketing as trackable, attributable spend, shows how case studies landed a dream client (UFC), and argues freelancers should fire abusive clients fast and price on value. He also makes the case that hiring a freelancer beats a full-time employee on cost.

chunks.heading: Marketing for results: performance marketing vs. brand spend
chunks.text:
Ross defines performance marketing as marketing with attribution: you can see where every sale came from. He contrasts it with brand-style marketing, where a company says "we spend 50 million a year" but cannot say what that returns.

- Brand-style spend: put in $50M, hope some sales appear, no data tying spend to outcome.
- Performance marketing: put in $10,000, track every click and every purchase, and report what came back out.
- Example he gives: a shop owner with a 15-year-old client list that has never been emailed. A $5,000 budget on an email to that list can return far more than it costs, and every spender and clicker is traceable.
- Results depend on the product and on how good the relationship with the audience is. He says there are "100 different variables."

chunks.heading: Winning large clients with case studies
chunks.text:
Ross used past results to land UFC as a client (signed the day of the interview).

- He showed case studies of what clients normally invest and how it typically works, rather than pitching in the abstract.
- He treats it as a test case: UFC gave only a tiny slice of its database, but he is running it through ActiveCampaign, where they pay full price for the platform and he gets a large return. His aim is that delivering well opens up the whole list (he guesses around 50 million people).
- He says he has generated over $150 million for clients in roughly five years, and earned over $2 million himself. He started on Upwork when people barely saw freelancing as a career.
- Authority assets: guest-contributed about 40 performance marketing articles to Entrepreneur (he had hoped for 10 a month; the publication is very strict), plus writing for Upwork and ActiveCampaign, and a Forbes feature.

chunks.heading: Client red flags: who he refuses to work with
chunks.text:
Ross became a freelancer partly because a former boss scammed him out of $75,000, so he screens clients hard.

His perfect client:
- doesn't try to negotiate on price
- understands his value
- doesn't demand things "tomorrow"
- plays by the rules, with mutual respect ("if you value me, I value you")

Red flags that get a client fired or refused:
- Pitches built on dubious ideas (for example, a person who bought a database and wants to push a crypto product that "tomorrow will be worth a million dollars").
- Mistreating their own staff. He fired a founder who had just sold a company to WeWork for about $12 million because of how he verbally abused his team: "I don't need your money, whereas the people who work for you do."
- Abusive behavior toward him. One client sent abusive messages every Wednesday. After the second occurrence he cut her off, even though her animation-video campaigns were making good sales.

His rule: "if you hit any red flag we're not going to work together, and no matter how much money you've got behind you, we're just not going to work." He sometimes turns down large offers on this basis.

chunks.heading: Cut bad clients quickly to protect your mental health
chunks.text:
- Ross says he built internal red flags over four to five years so he can cut people out fast.
- Bad clients "ruin your mental health," and the point of freelancing is a better work-life balance, higher pay and flexibility, not being treated badly.
- Observation on pricing and abuse: at lower hourly rates he got more abuse; at higher rates he got less himself, but saw high-paying clients abuse others. He took that as a signal about the client's character.
- Leading by example matters: how an owner treats staff affects everyone who relies on them.

chunks.heading: The business case for hiring a freelancer over a full-time employee
chunks.text:
Ross makes the cost argument for clients:
- A full-time hire in a place like Los Angeles at his skill level can cost roughly $400,000-$500,000 a year all-in (he says "4,000 maybe $500,000"; the transcript is unclear on the exact lower figure).
- A full-time employee also means insurance, equipment, maintenance and retirement contributions.
- A startup rarely has 40-60 hours a week of work for that role anyway. A freelancer can be used flexibly, on the hours actually needed, at a fraction of the cost.
- A freelancer can also be proactive, for example proposing "here's the email newsletter we should send this week."
- He wants freelancing to be seen as a legitimate model, and says the way people treat freelancers needs to evolve.

chunks.heading: Upwork, talent and reputation
chunks.text:
- Ross is critical of Upwork's early "high American talent" advertising. He argues there is nothing in a country's DNA that makes its talent better, and talent exists everywhere.
- Examples he gives: Ukrainians as strong designers, Filipinos as strong assistants (caring, good with numbers, good at timekeeping).
- He wants Upwork to educate clients about global talent and to screen out bad clients and bad freelancers more strictly.
- He says there are great clients and talent on Upwork: his clients there have included a UFC partner and someone who ran for US president.
- Reputation system: every client rating counts, so one negative review hurts, which is another reason he avoids clients he can't satisfy or who show red flags.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ross Jenkins, founder of a digital agency, argues email is among the cheapest and most measurable channels, and lays out five tactical fixes. Watch deliverability first, write for mobile, use one CTA, segment the list, and use humor in subject lines to earn opens.

chunks.heading: Deliverability is the first metric to watch
chunks.text:
- Ross argues deliverability rate is "one of the most overlooked, yet more important things" in email marketing. Open rate, click-through rate and revenue all matter, but "if nobody is receiving your emails, everything else is irrelevant."
- If a low percentage of the list reaches the inbox, or deliverability is dipping, he says to make changes quickly.
- Shared sending IPs are one risk. Some email platforms send from IP addresses that get flagged because some users spam. Other users then suffer from a "bad neighbor" sending from the same IPs.
- Spam filters are far more advanced than they used to be. They filter out what they consider junk based on spam-trigger words in the subject line and the email body.

chunks.heading: Write and design every email for mobile first
chunks.text:
- Ross says to assume every recipient will receive, open and read the message on a mobile device.
- Implications:
  - The subject line must grab attention right away.
  - The message must be direct and to the point.
  - The design must be eye-catching and flow seamlessly on a small screen.
- Mobile share is hard to pin down. Some sources claim more than 50% of emails are opened on mobile, others north of 70%. He expects the number to keep rising, so designing every campaign with mobile in mind is safe.
- A custom responsive email template is a low-cost way to make branded emails stand out.

chunks.heading: One call to action per email
chunks.text:
- Ross criticizes emails that leave the reader unsure what is being promoted. These often mix links to blog posts with random sales or promotions, giving "zero direction, zero clarity."
- He says such emails don't convert and push many people to unsubscribe.
- His rule: include a single call to action, and tell the recipient exactly what the action is and what you want them to do.
- Example: an apparel brand sending a pre-sale notification for a limited-edition drop. The email should make that purpose clear with:
  - A short text blurb.
  - An image of the product.
  - One large button reading "Pre-Order Now!"
- He says that is "all it takes to drive results."

chunks.heading: Segment the list instead of sending one message to everyone
chunks.text:
- Ross says sending the same message to the entire list leaves "a lot of money on the table" every time.
- He advises dividing the list into as many segments as possible, using whatever data fits the business, such as purchase history and order frequency.
- His underlying point: not all recipients want the same thing. The sooner a business accepts that, the sooner it can send emails that match what each group wants.
- Segmentation is not an overnight process. A simple start is two groups, customers and non-customers, then segmenting further from there.

chunks.heading: Subject lines: earn the open with humor and shock value
chunks.text:
- Ross says the recipient has to open the email before anything else matters. An excellent offer inside produces no return if the email is skipped or deleted.
- The subject line must command attention and trigger a click, and the email has to stand out from the dozens of others in the inbox.
- His recommendation is to experiment with humor and shock value in subject lines.
- Related warning: he links the "screamed advertisement" feel and weak subject lines to people hitting delete.

chunks.heading: Why email deserves real effort
chunks.text:
- Ross calls email marketing one of the most affordable and effective online-marketing strategies. It drives revenue with a click and keeps a strong relationship with customers and users.
- He says it is highly measurable, so campaigns can be optimized and fine-tuned to deliver ROI that outperforms all other marketing channels.
- His observation: many businesses put very little effort into email, "and it shows."
- His five improvements for the next campaign:
  1. Monitor deliverability.
  2. Optimize for mobile.
  3. Use a single CTA.
  4. Segment the list.
  5. Use humor and shock value in subject lines.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ross Jenkins argues raw traffic volume is a vanity metric and that traffic only matters if it converts to revenue. He breaks website traffic into five sub-metrics (unique visitors, bounce rate, referral sources, CPV/RPV, and page views/duration) so you can scale the best sources and cut the worst.

chunks.heading: Evaluating traffic by revenue, not volume
chunks.text:
Ross argues that website traffic only matters if it converts into revenue. "The name of the game is revenue. If your website traffic isn't converting into revenue, it's essentially worthless." He criticizes digital-marketing agencies that report raw traffic volume as success: "visits alone mean nothing."

- Break traffic down into sub-metrics to scale online growth.
- Once you know which traffic sources are most valuable, increase those efforts. Pull back on the lowest-performing sources.
- Ross lists five metrics to run an online campaign: unique visitors, bounce rate, referral traffic sources, CPV/RPV, and page views with average visit duration.

chunks.heading: Unique visitors as a campaign health check
chunks.text:
Ross treats total unique visitors per campaign as a starting point for deciding whether a campaign is worth continuing.

- A unique visit is counted once. If someone clicks a Facebook ad, lands on the site, and returns an hour later, the second visit is not counted.
- Raw visits can mislead. Example: a blog post drives 500 visits, but 300 are the same person, leaving 200 uniques.
- Track uniques over time per source. A steady decline signals the source is drying up and is less effective at introducing new people to the business.

chunks.heading: Using bounce rate to find disconnects
chunks.text:
Bounce rate measures visitors who leave without clicking to another page or taking an action such as submitting a form or completing a conversion goal.

- A high bounce rate suggests visitors aren't finding what they expected.
- Likely causes he names: an offer that overpromises and a site that underdelivers, poor user experience, or confusing navigation.
- Fix: install a heat-map tool to see where visitors click and how far they scroll, which helps locate the disconnect.

chunks.heading: Reverse-engineering referral sources by cost per conversion
chunks.text:
Ross says identifying every traffic source lets you reverse engineer which is most valuable in terms of revenue generated and cost per visit.

- Example: if one source delivers sales at a $15 conversion cost and another delivers the same traffic value at $8 per conversion, scale the cheaper source.
- Track organic Google traffic, referral visits from embedded links on other sites, and social media.
- When running multiple campaigns, use Google's UTM parameters to analyze all the data in Google Analytics.

chunks.heading: CPV and RPV for campaign profitability
chunks.text:
Cost-per-visitor (CPV) and revenue-per-visitor (RPV) show how profitable each campaign is, so you can budget and plan for growth. Ross says to know these numbers for every traffic source.

- RPV = revenue from a channel divided by visitors it drove. Example: a Facebook ads campaign with 100 tracked sales worth $10,000 and 1,000 visitors gives an RPV of $10 ($10,000 / 1,000).
- CPV = total dollars spent in a channel divided by the visitors it drove.
- Comparing CPV to RPV per channel tells you where to put budget.

chunks.heading: Page views and visit duration to guide optimization
chunks.text:
Ross recommends tracking pages viewed per visit, time on site per visit, and what visitors ultimately do (leave without acting, submit a form, make a purchase) in Google Analytics.

- Reverse engineer the actions that generate revenue to make better optimization decisions.
- If most conversions follow interaction with a specific content piece, send paid traffic directly to that content asset.
- If most conversions happen after a visitor stays at least three minutes, improve content and create more long-form articles to raise average visit duration.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ross Jenkins, founder of digital agency DigitalME, argues there is no best website platform, only the one that fits your goals. He walks through five filters: intended use, technical expertise, budget, design customization, and ease of updating. Cheap, mainstream platforms like Shopify and WordPress can carry very large businesses.

chunks.heading: Choosing a platform by fit, not by hype
chunks.text: Ross argues there is no one-size-fits-all website platform. Every business has different online objectives, products and services, so the goal is to find the platform that suits its specific needs. He warns against picking the "best option" according to "some random blogger who more than likely has an affiliate link or two slipped into the article." Far too often, businesses end up on a platform that isn't up to par for what they need, or build on something that is complete overkill. He frames the choice around five factors: intended use, technical expertise, budget, design customization and ease of updating.

chunks.heading: Match the platform to the website's intended use
chunks.text:
Ross starts with what the site needs to do.

- **Online presence only** (showcase products, services, company info): a WordPress site with a blog does the trick.
- **Direct-to-consumer selling:** Shopify is a plug-and-play option with low-cost plans and a very low barrier to entry.
- **Unique needs:** a fully custom build may be required.
- **No blogging and no SEO intent:** a simple single-page HTML website is enough.

He associates WordPress with blogs and small local businesses, and Shopify with ecommerce. Other players and fully custom builds also exist.

chunks.heading: Treat the website as a tool and invest in the skills to use it
chunks.text:
Ross says platforms demand different levels of technical expertise, and many people don't consider this. Time spent learning a platform helps you get the most out of the site. A live website is only a start, because it is a tool for the business.

- A Shopify store that connects a domain, uploads some products and then sits there "isn't going to grow quickly, if at all."
- Someone with more technical knowledge can use the tracking and insights to drive more sales.
- That person can also use abandonment recovery and upselling, among other things, to lift sales.

His point is that knowing how to leverage a website to its full potential can significantly affect business success.

chunks.heading: Budget ranges from nearly free to a quarter-million dollars
chunks.text:
Ross lays out the cost spectrum:

- **WordPress:** free to download, install and set up. Roughly $12 for a domain plus low-cost shared hosting at $5 per month.
- **Shopify:** build with a free template and be running for $29 per month.
- **Fully custom build:** custom databases, functionality and more. You could "drop a quarter-million dollars" on an elaborate one.

He cautions against discounting the low-cost options. They can handle large companies: some of the largest ecommerce brands in the world run on Shopify and generate millions of dollars daily on the same tech stack available to any small business.

chunks.heading: Decide how much design customization you actually need
chunks.text:
Ross says the level of customization determines the build path.

- **Modest needs:** both Shopify and WordPress offer free themes that work well and allow some customization.
- **Paid themes:** thousands are available, priced from $39 to $200. They give affordable access to sleek designs and features that can be adjusted to match your needs and branding.
- **Custom animation and unique design:** hire a front-end and back-end team to build from the ground up. This one-off customization "will cost a pretty penny," but for some businesses the expense is worth it.

chunks.heading: Favor platforms you can learn and update yourself
chunks.text:
Ross's final factor is ease of updating and the resources available. Popular DIY platforms such as Shopify, WordPress, BigCommerce, Wix and Squarespace all have plenty of online guidance, both from the platforms themselves (blog and video content) and from user-created content.

- If the budget doesn't cover an onsite development team to manage and update the site, pick a platform you feel comfortable and confident learning.
- He notes that today almost anything related to development can be found on YouTube.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ross Jenkins, founder of digital agency DigitalME, lays out seven basic LinkedIn tactics for sending traffic to a website: a credible profile, a large first-degree network, groups, steady posting, curiosity-driven link titles, and an RSS blog feed. The advice is generic and tactical, with no data from his own results.

chunks.heading: LinkedIn profile setup as the base of website traffic
chunks.text:
- Ross treats the profile as the first step in driving traffic from LinkedIn. It does not need to be complex, but it must cover the basics.
- A winning profile has three parts:
  - a clean, presentable headshot
  - a brief introduction of what you do
  - a concise, straight-to-the-point work history
- His reasoning is credibility: "the more organized and professional a profile is, the more credible it appears to a target audience."
- Context he cites: LinkedIn has 740 million members worldwide and almost 65 million in the U.S. A 2015 Recruiter Nation survey found 87% of recruiters use it to look for talent.
- He argues that few industry pros use LinkedIn as a route to website traffic, even though it can be one.

chunks.heading: Growing first-degree connections to widen reach
chunks.text:
- Ross says to build first-degree connections, meaning people you choose to accept as a connection.
- More connections expand the network and raise the chance of sending people to your website.
- The mechanism he gives: a higher connection count makes it more likely other users see you in their "most viewed connections" list. It also broadens reach, so more people see and click the website link on your profile.
- Target: start with at least 500 first-degree connections, then keep building.
- Three ways to keep building:
  - personalize connection requests
  - explore LinkedIn groups
  - engage more with your current connections

chunks.heading: Joining relevant LinkedIn groups
chunks.text:
- Ross recommends joining groups relevant to your industry for three reasons:
  - You can build and gain more connections there.
  - You can post your own content in the groups to entice target audiences to visit your site and see more of it.
  - You find and connect with like-minded people in your industry, which can further boost traffic.
- He notes that some groups have more than 500,000 members, which makes them useful for reach.

chunks.heading: Creating your own LinkedIn group
chunks.text:
- Ross suggests starting a group in addition to joining others. Benefits:
  - It establishes you as an expert in your industry.
  - The more people who join, the broader your reach and the more traffic you drive.
  - You can message members with helpful resources or articles from your website, which strengthens your expert reputation.
  - If members share those links with others in the industry, the traffic effect is amplified.
- He flags the cost: running a group means constantly engaging the audience. Ways to do that:
  - post content regularly
  - ask questions
  - comment on posts

chunks.heading: Posting frequency and content rhythm
chunks.text:
- Ross compares LinkedIn to Facebook and Twitter. The audience differs slightly, but the same principle applies: to drive traffic, give people a steady stream of engaging content.
- Share new content at least once a day. It can include images, videos and other striking elements. This keeps attention and entices people to visit your site for more.
- Avoid oversharing (posting too much or too often) and spamming, which he says "can have the opposite effect."
- Keep updates engaging and relevant, and post at a reasonable rate.

chunks.heading: Writing curiosity-driven link headlines
chunks.text:
- Ross calls engaging titles on links a proven traffic driver, because they pique curiosity and interest.
- Weak example: a link simply called "My Blog".
- Stronger examples:
  - "Boost Your Page Rankings with These X Tips"
  - "Top X Ways to Increase Your Website's Traffic"
- His rules for titles:
  - simple and concise
  - appeal to what the target audience is looking for
  - effectively summarize what they get by clicking

chunks.heading: Showing latest blog posts on your profile with an RSS feed
chunks.text:
- Ross recommends adding a Really Simple Syndication (RSS) feed to the profile. It displays your last couple of blog posts from your website.
- Steps as he describes them (this was LinkedIn's Applications feature in 2021):
  1. Go to the "Applications" section of your profile.
  2. Select the application you want under "Add an Application".
  3. Copy-paste your website's blog URL into the relevant field.
- Two benefits he names: it improves the look of the profile, and it gives visitors extra motivation to check out your site.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A generic beginner checklist for small-business marketing: plan first, build a website, show up on social media, claim your online listings, run a few targeted ads, network locally, use coupons and free trials, and stay consistent. Broad and light on specifics, but a usable starting list.

chunks.heading: Marketing as a competitive edge, not a product afterthought
chunks.text:
Ross Jenkins argues that high-quality products and services are no longer enough. A strong marketing game sets a business apart from competitors and pushes consumers to choose it. He notes that "there are a lot of brands out there with mediocre products and services, but they still find success as a result of their excellent marketing strategies."

- Marketing reaches a wider audience that may want the product and lifts later sales.
- It improves brand credibility, which makes consumer loyalty easier to win.
- Options range from traditional channels (TV, print, radio) to modern ones (social media).
- He says the hardest part is knowing where to start.
- He closes on consistency: people can't buy from a business they don't know exists, so the business has to keep making itself known.

chunks.heading: Start with a simple plan and an elevator statement
chunks.text:
Ross says any marketing effort starts with a plan, and the plan doesn't need to be big. What matters is that it is beneficial for ROI.

- Begin with brainstorming sessions, themes, lists of items and targets on a calendar.
- Write an elevator statement: what you want people to know about your brand, products or services in 30 seconds. It should be interesting.
