- Get feedback from people in advance as another way to refine the plan.
- The goal of whichever method is to create a good impression.

chunks.heading: Website, SEO and analytics basics
chunks.text:
Ross says many customers search for a business on Google, so a website lets them see what you offer.

- Build it yourself or hire a professional web-development agency. Hire a professional if you want more features.
- Focus on SEO and make the site work on different devices.
- Use Google Analytics to monitor traffic.
- Be wary of anyone who guarantees a top search ranking, "unless this person works as a developer for Google."

chunks.heading: Social media presence and claiming your business listings
chunks.text:
Ross advises being visible on social media to tap into different audiences.

- He says most of the traffic is on Facebook, and a business without a Facebook page may be missing opportunities.
- Social media use is growing, including among older people, who are there because their children, grandchildren, friends and former colleagues are.
- He also recommends claiming your business online. Information about a business can be found online regardless, and you want to control what people read about your products or services.
- Search your business in different browsers to see what is shared, then claim it by creating a business listing.

chunks.heading: Paid search with Google AdWords
chunks.text:
Ross recommends Google AdWords to target the specific products or services you sell.

- Choose a few quality keywords rather than a lot of them.
- AdWords lets you pick a target location and work within a budget.
- More broadly, if other methods aren't enough, advertise: show how you differ from competitors and how people can contact you.
- He says advertising is not one-size-fits-all, so figure out what works best for your business.

chunks.heading: Community involvement, networking and promotional items
chunks.text:
Ross says to build awareness locally by joining business associations, community organizations and groups. Anything that gets the business involved helps.

- Networking expands contacts, brings new referrals and raises awareness of the business.
- It also gets the attention of other business leaders.
- Support events and programs for a good cause. This makes the business known and helps the community.
- Give away promotional items carrying the business name, logo and contact information at these events.
- He singles out T-shirts as "free walking marketing."

chunks.heading: Coupons, free trials and protecting your content
chunks.text:
Ross suggests giving away coupons or free trials of products or services to start building followers.

- A satisfied customer returns and shares the experience with family and friends.
- Reach out to people you know to help promote the business.
- He also advises protecting ideas and content with copyright in a form the law recognizes. For printed material, he suggests obtaining federal copyright protection.
- If you invest heavily in a website, protect ownership of its contents, graphics and general design.
- He mentions agencies like Upwork as a way to get help with this.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ross Jenkins argues that buying an existing turnkey business beats starting from scratch because you inherit market research, a proven model, a loyal customer base and seller support. It is a generic, listicle-style case for acquisition over startup, with a closing reminder to do due diligence and consult experts before signing.

chunks.heading: Why Ross favors buying a turnkey business
chunks.text:
Ross defines a turnkey business as one that already exists and includes everything needed to operate. It is bought outright, and the buyer's only responsibility is managing it. He notes the preference for turnkey businesses has been rising and calls them "the best" route compared with starting from scratch.

- Starting from scratch means building everything; buying means stepping into a running operation.
- He frames the choice as getting value for money from a reliable, previously proven model.

chunks.heading: Skipping market research and using a proven model
chunks.text:
- A new business needs extensive market research on the target audience and what they like. A turnkey business removes that work because it has been in the market (often at the same location) for a while, so the buyer inherits insight into customers.
- Ross says to start due diligence by reviewing the business's full inventory records. They show regular purchasing cost and how quickly stock moves.
- A turnkey business is a proven model that removes the guesswork new entrepreneurs face when choosing a strategy to maximize profit.
- It has a "predetermined play" the new owner can follow.
- These models are replicable and simple enough for a new owner to manage.
- They come with existing customer loyalty and built-in awareness.

chunks.heading: Speed and ease of setup
chunks.text:
- Starting a business involves many complex, lengthy factors. Turnkey businesses, especially mobile concepts, are quick to start because they don't need an extensive hiring process or a pricey build-out.
- Most hire only one or two people, with the entrepreneur operating the business. The owner can add staff as the business grows.
- As a franchise, a turnkey business skips steps like selecting the optimal site and constructing a building, so it begins making money sooner.
- It has an active sales unit with equipment and systems already in place.

chunks.heading: Seller support and an established customer base
chunks.text:
- When selling, most owners offer "unlimited support" to the new owner. Ross lists technology, marketing, training and operations optimization as areas of help, and calls this what sets turnkey apart from other businesses.
- Partnering with a supportive franchisor improves the odds of steering the business in the right direction.
- Ross argues the hardest part of any business is getting people to switch from a competitor's product, which typically means proving your brand is best and offering hefty discounts.
- A turnkey business has an already established, loyal customer base, so the product or service has a ready market. This improves the odds of success.

chunks.heading: Cost, fees and room to grow
chunks.text:
- Most turnkey businesses have no specific rules, guidelines or limitations, so the owner can grow without constraint.
- Caveat: some turnkey franchise models have regulations that protect the brand name, which the buyer must follow under the contract.
- The initial investment is substantial, but Ross says you get value for every penny. If you can afford it, expansion is easy, which matters most for first-time owners.
- It helps with multi-unit franchising: avoid paying unending fees and manually setting up branches from scratch.
- He says turnkey businesses rarely have hidden fees or continuous fees, and are highly unlikely to charge marketing fees or land royalties.
- A well-established business with a solid customer base saves the marketing costs and promotional offers needed to attract new customers when starting from zero.

chunks.heading: Due diligence before buying
chunks.text:
- Ross cautions not to settle for the first turnkey business you come across.
- Conduct thorough research.
- Schedule a consultation with the current business owners before signing a contract.
- Consult experts to help with the search so you choose the right turnkey business.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ross Jenkins, founder of a digital agency, gives a practical checklist for hiring remote freelancers. It covers sourcing through referrals and multiple marketplaces, writing precise job listings, screening with a simple qualifier, video calls, references and test tasks, and moving fast to remove bad hires.

chunks.heading: Sourcing referrals before marketplaces
chunks.text:
- Ross's first move for a remote hire is to email and text fellow entrepreneurs and friends. Many businesses went fully remote, so his circle likely has talent sources and recommendations.
- Screening effort should match the role. A remote content writer producing a few blog posts a month needs a much lighter qualification process than a back-end developer for a SaaS company. The two are "two completely different approaches."
- He calls a few emails and texts to his entrepreneurial circle "a great starting point."

chunks.heading: Posting on multiple freelance marketplaces
chunks.text:
- Ross says never limit the search to one marketplace, because many talented candidates don't register on all of them.
- He names Freelancer, UpWork and Toptal as the major players and recommends creating a profile and posting the requirements on each.
- The goal is the largest possible talent pool. He calls it the "lazy route" to assume the site you think is best will have what you need.
- The extra effort is worth it, and detailed listings help cut low-quality applicants.

chunks.heading: Defining job requirements and qualifications up front
chunks.text:
- The clearer the description of the role, expectations, qualifications and duties, the better qualified the applicants.
- Clear listings also reduce unqualified applicants clogging the inbox.
- A generic listing draws interest from a very broad range of talent. Ross says to spell out exactly what you want and don't want.
- Detailed listings that state both wants and don't-wants limit low-quality applicants and bring talent aligned with the need.
- Context: demand for freelancers and remote workers spiked as companies went remote after the pandemic, bringing top talent but also an influx of unqualified applicants.

chunks.heading: Screening freelancers with a qualifier, video call, references and tests
chunks.text:
Ross says remote hiring still needs a thorough interview process. His steps:

- **Qualifier in the application.** Ask candidates to upload a 60-second YouTube video explaining why they are the best fit, and include the link in their response. "If they cannot follow a simple instruction, delete them, as they are not attentive to details."
- **Always do a video call.** Nothing gives a better feel for who someone is than seeing and interacting with them face-to-face.
- **Confirm references.** Contact past employers by simple email or phone call. This can surface issues or drawbacks that don't show up right away.
- **Give test assignments.** "Anyone can look good on paper." Tests show how someone performs in the real world and with your team.

chunks.heading: Hire slow, fire fast
chunks.text:
- Ross calls this "the most important tip."
- Take your time hiring and don't feel rushed. There is a lot of talent available and it may take a while to sift through.
- Mistakes happen. Sometimes a hire turns out to be the opposite of who you thought.
- When that happens, fire fast. The longer a bad fit stays, the more damage they do. He describes such a person as a "cancerous team member" to remove from the equation as quickly as possible.

chunks.heading: Why remote teams are now mainstream
chunks.text:
- Ross notes remote teams aren't new, and many startups have long run this way, but the pandemic made the model more widespread, adaptable and accepted.
- Companies kept operating virtually even as areas reopened, for three reasons he cites: they learned a remote workforce is workable, employees like remote work and are more productive, and there are cost savings.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ross Jenkins compares UFC's centralized, fighter-persona-driven, digital-first model with boxing's fragmented promoter model and print/PPV reach. He draws marketing and business lessons on brand control, storytelling, fair pay for brand reputation, and using digital channels for younger audiences.

chunks.heading: UFC's business model and how it markets
chunks.text:
Ross describes UFC as "one big brand" that follows the business model of pro wrestling. It promotes fighters by building their personas and stories rather than promoting the events themselves, which he calls an effective way to draw more people in.

- UFC is a single entity controlling promotions, regulations, contracts, broadcasts and the sanctioning body.
- It sets a fixed price for every fighter, and even fighter bonuses are fixed.
- UFC decides who fights whom, so fighters cannot cherry-pick opponents.
- Fighters mostly just follow through with the marketing strategy, and because the focus is on their stories, they are more engaged with fans.
- Because everything is produced in-house, UFC as a whole earns more, though the same is not true of its fighters.
- The downside for fighters: they have to pitch themselves to UFC to get hired, so their pay can be smaller than a boxer's.

chunks.heading: Boxing's fragmented model and promoter dynamics
chunks.text:
Boxing is made up of many entities, with different promoters and sanctioning bodies. Ross contrasts it with UFC on who approaches whom and who controls the product.

- Promoters usually scout boxers and convince them to sign, rather than boxers pitching themselves.
- Once signed, the promoter sets up the boxer's fights. The price of promotion is a deal between the boxer's team and the promoting team.
- The promoter and manager have a say in whether a fight happens.
- Because the boxers are the product, their teams protect the boxer's legacy. Ross concludes that is why big fights rarely happen: "Each side is working hard to promote its title."
- Boxing has a clearer set of rules and, having been around so long, has produced legends.

chunks.heading: Boxing's traditional distribution channels
chunks.text:
Ross says boxing leans on traditional media and live attendance, which suits its more traditional audience.

- Promotion is mostly in print (newspapers and sports magazines, in digital or physical form), plus radio and talk shows.
- Fights rely on live viewings at the MGM Grand, often with full seats.
- Fights air on Showtime PPV and ESPN+ by pay-per-view, and companies can advertise in between the fights.
- He calls boxing more accessible and more old school than UFC.

chunks.heading: UFC's digital-first distribution and pricing
chunks.text:
Ross notes UFC focuses on digital media and draws more viewership from younger adults.

- Following its recent deal, UFC fights are broadcast on ESPN+.
- Each pay-per-view costs $70, on top of the monthly and yearly ESPN+ subscriptions.
- UFC uses social media to promote fighters and events.

chunks.heading: How Ross says UFC could improve: pay fairly and allow sponsorships
chunks.text:
Ross argues UFC's strategy is solid but needs tweaks to be as stable as boxing.

- Pay fighters more. His reasoning: people are very conscious of what they buy, and if a product wasn't sourced ethically, they drop it even if they like it. The same applies to UFC.
- He says the impending lawsuit hurts the brand UFC is trying to create, and that "fighters should be paid fairly for their hard work."
- Allow fighters more sponsorships and deals. He argues restricting them can cost UFC opportunities from ad revenues.

chunks.heading: How Ross says UFC could improve: use digital marketing more fully
chunks.text:
Ross's second recommendation is to exploit digital marketing more, given UFC's younger audience.

- Both sports are combat sports but have different audiences. Boxing's traditional audience is reached through traditional marketing, while UFC's younger audience sits online.
- UFC already uses social media, but he says it could optimize its use of different digital-marketing tools.
- His conclusion: "Utilizing every aspect of digital marketing will help UFC leverage the sport."

chunks.heading: General marketing lessons from the comparison
chunks.text:
- Marketing plays a key role in why people show up to see athletes in the first place, even when they come for the fighters and their sportsmanship.
- Stories sell: every champion has a great story to tell, and promoting the persona and story (UFC's approach) pulls in more people than promoting the event.
- Match the channel to the audience: traditional print, radio and live attendance for an older audience, digital and social for a younger one.
- Owning the whole value chain (UFC) maximizes the organization's earnings and control, but can create friction and reputational risk with the people who create the product.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ross Jenkins uses Jake Paul as a case study for businesses. Key takeaways: appreciate your customers, build a recognizable brand, set high targets, believe in your offer, and use sponsorships (financial or in-kind) to borrow an influencer's audience. It is a high-level listicle with little concrete data.

chunks.heading: Jake Paul as a marketing playbook: appreciate your audience and put them first
chunks.text:
Ross Jenkins uses Jake Paul (then 24, a Vine-born social-media personality who moved to the Disney show _Bizaardvark_, music, YouTube and an undefeated boxing run) as a case study in how businesses should market themselves. He treats Paul's methods, "however polarizing they may sometimes be", as having made him "a household name across the country and even worldwide".

- Ross says clients are the reason a business prospers. Show them they are the reason you have made it this far.
- He points to Paul's appreciation of his viewers and fans as a standout trait. Paul credits his boxing career to the support and encouragement of fans on YouTube and other platforms.
- Tactic: when Paul plans an event, he makes sure his audience hears the news first. Ross applies this to business: give your existing customers announcements before anyone else.
- Paul uses the internet and his YouTube following (millions of followers) to advertise upcoming events. Ross notes this has grown his sports popularity and the view counts on his videos.

chunks.heading: Build your personal and company brand without fear
chunks.text:
Ross argues that a business must get noticed in order to grow, and that founders should not be afraid to build up their own name because it helps growth and sales.

- Paul "became famous because he always came up with new ways to market his brand".
- He built his brand by doing business differently and embracing the controversies that made him more famous.
- Ross's framing: "bad publicity is still publicity". Controversy around Paul has not stopped him finding success in his various endeavors, which is why Ross calls him a marketing playbook for businesses.
- Ross notes Paul's sustained fame (still gaining popularity "day in and day out") despite the controversies, and treats it as evidence the approach works, whether people love or hate him.
- Takeaway: do business differently, stay visible, and keep inventing fresh ways to promote the brand.

chunks.heading: Set high targets and have plans to succeed
chunks.text:
Ross credits Paul with always aiming high.

- Paul's stance, as Ross relays it: do not let yourself fail. Set targets that guarantee more returns in the business.
- Ross frames this as having concrete plans and goals tied to returns, rather than drifting.
- Paul's trajectory (Vine video, a Disney TV role, being fired from the show, then exploring music and boxing) is used to show that setbacks can free up creativity to try new ventures. Ross says being fired "allowed him to explore his creativity more".

chunks.heading: Believe in your offer and be ready to support it
chunks.text:
Ross pairs two mindset and preparation points.

- **Believe in yourself:** when you are set to do something, go for it and do not let anything discourage you. For a business to prosper, you have to believe that what you offer is the best in the market at that time.
- **Support your business:** be ready to back your business when you introduce yourself to the market, whatever the product or service.
- Be prepared with helpful information about your product or brands whenever you pitch or introduce them.

chunks.heading: Use sponsorships: financial and in-kind
chunks.text:
Ross calls sponsorship a strategy Paul uses and "the majority of influencers use nowadays", and recommends finding the right sponsors for your content to improve your chances of online success.

- **Financial sponsorship:** influencers are paid so they can keep making content. Common on YouTube, for example when a creator suddenly diverts a video to talk about a particular product.
- **In-kind sponsorship:** usually product-placement advertising, common on Instagram and Facebook, where creators promote products in stories and posts. Creators must now indicate that such posts contain paid advertising, so they are easy to spot.
- **Why companies sponsor figures like Paul:** it is a win-win. By using a large influencer following they increase brand awareness and credibility.
- Paul's popularity and influence in the business world attracted many parties willing to strike deals and offer him sponsorship.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ross Jenkins, founder of DigitalME, gives five practical time management habits for freelancers. He covers goal visualization, ranking work by value and urgency, logging tasks on a calendar, removing distractions, and refusing work to avoid burnout. The advice is generic but reflects a stability-over-volume mindset.

chunks.heading: Visualizing goals to direct time and attention
chunks.text:
Ross treats visualization as the first step after a business idea is conceived. It answers where you see yourself, what your goals are and how you'll achieve them. He argues it puts the brain in "focus" mode so later actions aim at one purpose: making the vision real.

- He applies it to time management by tying daily work to a concrete goal, for example "getting 10 new clients by the end of next month."
- Tactic: place goal reminders where they stay visible every day, such as a dashboard or a sticky note in the workplace.
- Reading the same goal message each morning orients how you spend your time toward achieving it.

chunks.heading: Prioritizing activities when you control your own hours
chunks.text:
Ross notes that freelancers have complete freedom over working hours, which can lead to confusion. Freedom to choose hours does not mean overlapping activities. His rule: complete the most important activities first, then the next ones.

- If prioritizing is hard, list all recurring and pending activities in order of importance.
- With simultaneous jobs, decide which is more valuable. That can be the highest-paying job, or the one needing immediate attention where not finishing it could hurt your career.
- Then list pending tasks for each job and start with the most critical.
- Activities that are neither important nor urgent can be deleted or archived indefinitely until everything else is done.

chunks.heading: Building a written schedule and task log
chunks.text:
Once priorities are set, Ross says to write all tasks down (on paper or computer) and put pending activities on a calendar with what needs doing and the deadline for each.

- Include details for each item. Example: for a new-client meeting, record the place, time, how long it will take and what it is about.
- Track a status for every task: pending, completed, or not yet started.
- Keeping a task log lets you measure your productivity.
- If writing things down isn't enough, he recommends online task-organizing tools, some of them free.

chunks.heading: Removing distractions from the work environment
chunks.text:
Ross says even the smallest distractions subconsciously divert you, so you should detect and eliminate them, or develop strategies to ignore them.

- He names social media as one of the top distractions for freelancers, who spend most of their time in front of a screen and keep checking notifications during work hours, which can severely damage productivity.
- Use tools that block social media during working hours.
- Choose a workplace used exclusively for freelance work, so it is impossible to do something different there.
- Move unrelated hobby gear out of the workspace. His example: a freelance writer who paints in spare time should move the painting tools to a separate room.

chunks.heading: Protecting capacity: don't overwork and learn to say no
chunks.text:
Ross says to take only the jobs you can handle. Overloading leads to bad results, which can damage client relationships in the long term. He has "seen many cases of freelancers abandoning their quests because they were burned out and didn't deliver their work on time."

- Beginners tend to accept as many jobs as possible, believing there won't be second chances. He argues the primary goal should instead be finding something stable they can hold in the long run.
- A necessary freelancing skill is rejecting jobs when you know you lack the time: "Learn to say 'no' when you don't have the time for the job."
- Work-life balance matters, and as a freelancer you are the one in charge and the one who sets your own schedule.
- He calls mental health one of the key aspects of a successful career, achieved through proper time management.

chunks.heading: Why time management underpins a sustainable freelance career
chunks.text:
Ross frames time management as "one of the most critical factors for building a successful career," because time is a limited resource.

- He describes successful freelancers as experienced people who know how to land the next job after finishing one, build connections with long-term clients, and, most importantly, manage their time.
- His context: after the pandemic pushed businesses online and millions of workers home, freelancing opportunities grew, and he sees the freelancers who last as those who manage time well.
- His five-part approach: visualize goals, prioritize activities, build a schedule, remove distractions, and avoid overwork.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A practical checklist for new freelancers on getting hired. It covers listing on platforms, tapping personal networks, narrowing your niche, staying responsive, earning repeat work, and bringing in collaborators honestly.

chunks.heading: Choosing a freelance niche and platform presence
chunks.text:
- Ross says to sell your service "in a place full of people who need it": create profiles on several freelance platforms (Upwork is his example) to widen your connections and get your name out.
- A strong profile lists skill sets, experience, education, portfolio and basic information, so clients can judge fit. Clients may also ask extra questions before hiring.
- He notes that platform traffic matters for getting hired, but "it all boils down to how you 'sell' yourself to employers."
- He calls being too broad a common mistake. A profile that says only "writer" or "graphic artist" is unattractive, because most clients want someone who can do a specific job repeatedly, not a vague one.
- His fix is to sell within a niche. A writer could position as "children's blog writing" or "informative article writing."

chunks.heading: Do not rely on platforms alone: use your personal network
chunks.text:
- Ross tells freelancers not to depend only on the platforms they've joined.
- Make your services known to people you know personally: acquaintances, relatives, friends and friends' friends all become potential clients.
- Personal contacts already know your skills and output, so they have "little to no doubt" about you.
- He says never to underestimate direct family and friends as a source of recommendations and referrals that bring more clients.

chunks.heading: Being active, responsive and priced sensibly when starting out
chunks.text:
- Ross argues you cannot create an account and wait. A new, inexperienced freelancer with an idle profile will lose clients, so you must do the pursuing and apply for gigs on the platform.
- When new, consider a lower hourly rate than most freelancers, but not too low, because clients may then assume you only produce subpar work. His rule: "Make it reasonable, yet lower than most freelancers."
- Respond as fast as possible to client queries and stay professional and polite.
- After being hired, give frequent updates to reassure the client the project is moving and will be delivered on time.

chunks.heading: Winning repeat work from existing clients
chunks.text:
- Ross says to meet or exceed each client's expectations. When you deliver, tell the client you're open to working with them again.
- This only works if the job was done well, so always produce high-standard work.
- If a client's project turns out to need more work than first specified, create a new project with new objectives instead of stretching the old one.
- If clients are thoroughly impressed by earlier work, they are likely to trust you with what follows.

chunks.heading: Collaborating honestly on projects too big to handle alone
chunks.text:
- Ross warns against overconfidence and overworking yourself. If a client hires you for a big project you can't do alone, tell the client you'll need to work with someone else.
- Do not take the credit yourself, because it "will backfire."
- He says clients "highly value honesty and transparency." Bringing in the right people to finish excellently shows commitment to quality, not weakness, so there's little reason for a client to decline.

chunks.heading: Long-term view: from freelancer to your own platform or company
chunks.text:
- Ross frames the six steps (join a platform, publicize, specify a niche, stay active and responsive, seek repeat work, collaborate openly) as simple but effective for attracting clients.
- He expects that, over time, a freelancer becomes self-sufficient and may have the means to build their own platform or company to showcase and sell their services to potential clients.
- He stresses that success is not overnight: you can't wait for a miracle, you must "work with what you have and actively pursue your goals one step at a time."
- He notes freelancing is hard, with roughly as many people failing as succeeding, but offers benefits such as working at your own pace and widening your professional network.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A 2021 Entrepreneur op-ed arguing that founders should invest early in digital tools. Covers cloud tools to cut overhead, communication and task-management software, brand-building apps, and analytics, SEO and CRM tools for lead generation. General and tool-focused, with few concrete numbers or tactics.

chunks.heading: Cost savings from cloud and digital tools
chunks.text:
- Ross says founders resist spending on digital tools, especially early on, but that focus on avoiding expenses makes them overlook what the tools offer. There is "a digital tool for just about everything," from customer interaction to internal coordination to market research.
- His argument: adopting current technology early creates "more chances for integration, development and prosperity" later.
- Cloud storage and cloud computing let a business run without office space, which means zero utility expenses. He frames this as especially relevant as remote work grows.
- Closing logic: these tools save time and may remove the need for extra hires, freeing time and budget to expand.

chunks.heading: Communicating with customers and staff
chunks.text:
- Ross recommends workplace-communication platforms to keep staff informed, and internal company email for frequent, important updates to the whole team.
- He says these tools help hold staff accountable and keep everyone moving the same way.
- For customers, he calls email a strong channel for regular news, special offers, or general company updates sent to the client list.

chunks.heading: Choosing task and project-management software
chunks.text:
- Ross says task-management tools range from standard time-management systems to paperwork and analytics functions. What they share is helping you "get more done in less time."
- Most are cloud-based, so people in different locations can collaborate from a computer or mobile device.
- Features differ, and most are paid, so he advises deciding which tasks you need help with before buying. Example: for a remote team, pick project software with strong collaboration features.

chunks.heading: Building brand awareness with digital tools
chunks.text:
- Ross defines brand awareness as market recognition of your business and products, ranging from customers remembering your name to clearly understanding what sets you apart from competitors.
- His reasoning: a strong, reputable brand is critical, because you cannot grow clients and revenue if the target audience does not know you.
- Visual marketing is central to brand building in the social media era. He points to Canva, which offers templates for social-media images, status updates and other visuals.
- He also suggests social-media-management tools to post to many profiles at once and optimize digital content.

chunks.heading: Expanding the market with analytics, SEO and CRM
chunks.text:
- Ross says growing a market takes more than email and social: use inventive technology that gives an edge in lead generation.
- Google Analytics is a "must-have" for tracking site traffic, internal links and the regions visitors come from.
- Paid all-in-one SEO programs can analyze organic-search rankings for your keywords and show what rivals have done.
- CRM software, built to manage customer relationships, is an option he recommends for expanding the customer base.

chunks.heading: How to pick tools
chunks.text:
- Ross notes busy owners juggle many responsibilities, and tools, services and platforms exist to help run the business.
- His process: first decide what you want to accomplish, then spend time researching the best solutions for that goal.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ross Jenkins lays out a tactical playbook for doubling freelance income on Upwork: send more proposals, respond fast, add income streams (consultations, productized catalog projects), push for weekly retainers, target long-term clients, and raise rates yearly. The advice is marketplace-specific but the funnel and pricing logic is general.

chunks.heading: Doubling Upwork income: proposal volume and responsiveness
chunks.text:
- Ross says sending more proposals is one of the most effective ways to earn more on Upwork. His funnel logic: more proposals lead to more interviews, more interviews lead to more jobs.
- His worked example: 10 proposals produce two interviews, and one interview becomes a job. Bidding on only five jobs might have missed the client he actually signed.
- Volume also builds skill. More practice writing proposals and interviewing means he lands a higher share of the jobs he pursues.
- He still reads job descriptions closely and only spends Connects on jobs that fit his work and income goals.
- When proposal volume rises, replies rise too, so he checks his Messages inbox throughout the day.
  - He works with clients in many time zones and uses the Upwork desktop and mobile apps to stay responsive.
  - He doesn't reply in the middle of the night, but shifts his hours a bit earlier or later when clients are likely in the office.
  - He checks notifications for interview invitations and periodically reviews "My Stats" (under "Find Work") to confirm he answers every invite within 24 hours.
- Before any of this, he keeps the profile current: specialized profiles, certifications, location, portfolio items. He also works toward Talent Badges (he holds Expert-Vetted).

chunks.heading: Building multiple income streams on Upwork
chunks.text:
- Ross says doubling income within 12 months means actively cultivating new opportunities, not just bidding more. He uses all three channels Upwork offers:
  1. Proposals through Talent Marketplace.
  2. Paid consultations.
  3. Productized services listed in Project Catalog.
- Paid consultations earn in two ways:
  - One-time fees from clients who want to pick his brain.
  - A route to being hired as a long-term partner on bigger projects, because clients pay to learn about him and his services.
- Clients find consultation offers through search filters, but only if consultations are switched on in the profile. He calls it a quick change that adds money every month.
- He admits most of his income still comes from sending proposals and accepting interview invites, but Project Catalog income is growing.
- Catalog projects are not passive income, since he still does the work. The upside is that clients can buy at any time, and he sometimes wakes up to new project requests without sending a proposal.
- Listing services isn't enough on its own. He keeps sending proposals and collecting testimonials and talent badges, and over time catalog projects become a larger share of income.

chunks.heading: Weekly retainer contracts for steady income
chunks.text:
- Ross proposes weekly-payment (retainer-style) contracts to smooth out fluctuating income, which worries many new independents.
- Example: a client pays $500 per week for five hours of availability. He is paid the $500 every week even if the client needs fewer than five hours.
- If a week runs over, he bills the extra hours hourly on top. Eight hours worked means three hours billed through the work diary plus the usual $500.
- Upwork proposals normally ask for an hourly rate or fixed project price, so he raises the weekly arrangement with the client during the interview.

chunks.heading: Using search filters to find long-term, steady-revenue jobs
chunks.text:
- Ross says top Upwork users use search filters deliberately. First decide how long a client relationship you want and how much work you can take on.
- Filter choices he describes:
  - Project length "less than one month" for a few hours a week and a new client alongside existing work.
  - Project length "more than 6 months" for dependable long-term income.
  - Hours "more than 30 hrs/week" if you want to work with one client at a time.
- He combines these with other filters, such as job type, to get curated lists matching his length and pay criteria.
- His income structure: one or more steady long-term clients form a solid revenue base, then he builds on top with one-off projects, shorter contracts and booked paid consultations.

chunks.heading: Saving profitable searches and using Job Digests
chunks.text:
- After a filter combination lands good clients, Ross saves the search ("save search", upper right) so he can return to it.
- Example search: "YouTube channel video editing" jobs, intermediate skill level, paying at least $50 per hour.
- Saved searches feed Upwork Job Digests, which deliver relevant jobs to his inbox. The more profitable searches he saves, the more relevant the digests.
- Job Digests are only available to Rising Talent, Top Rated, Top Rated Plus or Expert Vetted freelancers, which he cites as another reason to pursue those badges.

chunks.heading: Enterprise jobs and Talent Clouds
chunks.text:
- Ross recommends applying to Enterprise client jobs. If hired, you may be added to that company's Talent Cloud, a subset of the marketplace for one Enterprise client's jobs and the talent they know and trust.
- Talent Cloud jobs can be any duration, not necessarily long-term. Many Enterprise clients post directly into their Talent Clouds, so membership gives first access to work that may never reach the standard Talent Marketplace.
- If no Enterprise jobs appear in the marketplace, he suggests watching the inbox for Enterprise invites. As your profile and expertise grow, they may find you.

chunks.heading: Raising your rates regularly
chunks.text:
- Ross treats regular rate increases as part of growing revenue and says freelancers often overlook it, since cost of living rises each year.
- Factors that justify a raise:
  - Recent investment of time or money in developing skills and expertise.
  - New clients and projects over the past year, which grow the portfolio.
- His example: moving from $80 to $100 per hour is a 25% revenue increase with no extra hours worked.
- He points to Upwork's rate calculator for working out what to charge, especially if rates haven't moved in a while.
- His closing advice: make one change from the list, evaluate its impact, and keep decisions aligned with goals (income, professional path, client load, work-life balance).

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ross Jenkins, founder of DigitalME, lists eight behaviors that get freelancers banned on Upwork, such as off-platform chats and billing, fake reviews, and padded hours. The practical takeaway for running a freelance or agency business is to protect your platform account, keep payment protection, and build reputation through real client work.

chunks.heading: Off-platform contact is banned until a contract starts
chunks.text:
- Ross says chatting with prospects on WhatsApp, by phone, or via emails or phone numbers posted in job posts breaks the Upwork Terms of Service.
- His reasoning: off-platform it is easier for a scammer to ask for personal or banking details, and harder to report them. Calls should be started through Upwork, so Upwork can help if someone tries to scam or take advantage of him.
- Communication outside Upwork (such as a shared Slack channel) is fine only once a contract has started. He notes many clients still keep chatting on Upwork during a project because files and communication stay in one place.
- His script when a prospect asks to move off-platform: say he can only chat on Upwork until a contract starts.
  - A genuinely innocent client (often new to Upwork) agrees without argument. Some have thanked him for flagging the rules.
  - "If they keep pushing, I won't work with them."

chunks.heading: Always invoice through Upwork, and why the protections matter
chunks.text:
- Invoicing a client off-platform, or getting added to their payroll, after meeting on Upwork breaks the terms and can get an account shut down.
- Ross also treats it as a risk. Upwork's setup protects freelancers:
  - **Fixed price:** the client funds the first milestone up front. Upwork holds it in escrow and releases it when the job is done, which avoids clients who run off without paying.
  - **Hourly:** the client pays after approving logged time. If they don't, Upwork still pays for work that qualifies for hourly payment protection.
- Ross finds the setup "really brilliant for everyone", both as a freelancer and as an Upwork client himself. He can always reach Upwork support, and never has to hand out bank card or account details.
- The one exception is the conversion process, where the client pays a conversion fee to take the relationship off-platform. Only then can he invoice directly or join their non-Upwork payroll. Upwork support checks with the freelancer too, and he is under no obligation to agree.

chunks.heading: Never manipulate reviews or ratings
chunks.text:
- It is fine to ask a real client for a review (Upwork also reminds clients).
- Ross lists what gets accounts banned:
  - Creating a second account, posing as a client, and "hiring" your own profile.
  - Having friends or family hire you, real or fake, just to leave five stars.
  - Applying to scam posts that promise five-star reviews in exchange for Amazon reviews, YouTube clicks, social follows or PayPal transactions.
  - Threatening to withhold finished work or leave negative feedback unless the client rates you well.
  - Paying or bribing clients for good reviews.
- His position: "The best way to get good feedback on your Upwork profile is by doing high-quality work for real clients." That is also the only way to build Job Success Score and reach Top Rated status or higher.

chunks.heading: Don't pass off work that isn't yours (subcontractors are fine)
chunks.text:
- Ross distinguishes this from subcontracting. Teams and agencies are allowed on Upwork.
- His example: he runs an agency, DigitalME, and works with several business managers through Upwork. They are part of his agency and he pays them through Upwork to help on client projects.
- What is not allowed is claiming rights or originality you don't have:
  - Buying a personal-use Canva template on Etsy and telling the client you created it.
  - Removing watermarks from stock footage you didn't buy and delivering it.
- On AI: some projects may require disclosing AI use, and generative tools like Stable Diffusion can produce borderline copyright-infringing images. Ross errs on the side of caution and uses these tools "for inspiration, not final products".

chunks.heading: Use your real identity and never share your account
chunks.text:
- **Real name and photo:** a fake name or generic profile image can get an account suspended. Ross's analogy is that you wouldn't do business with people wearing ski masks or paper bags over their heads. Clients want to know they are working with a real person they can trust.
- **Privacy is still possible.** Profile visibility has three levels:
  - Public: visible to everyone and indexable by search engines (helpful for visibility).
  - Upwork users only: visible to logged-in clients, not indexed by search engines.
  - Private: visible only to someone you send a direct link to.
- Upwork also hides your full last name until you interact with a client, for example by sending a proposal or exchanging messages.
- **Never let anyone else use your talent profile.** Agency and client profiles can have multiple users, but a talent profile must be only you. Someone else could deliver low-quality work, break the terms or run a scam. Sharing login details also exposes your personal information, clients and finances. Even a stranger or someone you know with a "story" should be sent to Upwork support instead.

chunks.heading: Log hours honestly
chunks.text:
- Padding hours risks losing account privileges.
- Clients can allow manual time logging without Upwork's desktop tracker. If you use that option, track hours separately in a tool such as Everhour or Toggl and log only hours actually worked.
- Ross logs manually. He is "fully transparent beforehand with clients" about how and why he logs that way.
- His recommended default is Upwork's desktop app: no need to transfer hours between trackers, and it is simple to use.

chunks.heading: Avoid illegal or shady jobs and services
chunks.text:
- Ross's benchmark: if a job or service is generally illegal or widely regarded as shady, don't do it through Upwork.
- His list (not exhaustive):
  - Helping people cheat on tests or writing students' essays.
  - Sexually explicit content, child exploitation, or asking children to do any work (even a legitimate child-actor search).
  - Mining or scraping data that isn't yours to collect.
  - Fake profiles or "bot" followers.
  - Fake reviews (on or off Upwork).
  - Fake news reports.
  - Hacking any person or system.
  - Exposing private individuals' details or researching them for others.
  - Phishing tools or phishing attempts.
  - Violent content or threats.
- If someone offers or requests this kind of work, don't engage. Flag the content or message to Upwork and let them review it.

chunks.heading: Context behind the advice
chunks.text:
- Ross runs DigitalME, a digital marketing and CRM automation agency. He is a marketing expert (HubSpot, ActiveCampaign, Memberium certified) and ranked #1 on Upwork for digital marketing and CRMs.
- He says it's possible to build a business and a "great livelihood" on Upwork, and that he has done it.
- His growth path after protecting the account: build a dream client list, create great client experiences, and double income.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ross Jenkins, founder of marketing agency DigitalME, argues that during Covid19 a business can either cut costs and wait or transform by automating. He uses a gym example (online sessions, a lead-magnet freebie, email list, pre-sold packages, membership site) and warns against DIY automation. Short and promotional, with one useful funnel pattern.

chunks.heading: Pandemic response: automate the business instead of cutting costs
chunks.text: Ross frames the Covid-19 market as having two options for a struggling business. One is cutting costs and raising funding to buy time until the storm passes. He calls this "rather unrealistic" unless the business sells something like hand sanitizer. The other is to "push your boundaries and absolutely transform your business by automating it." He backs the second option, drawing on about 10 years of running his marketing agency DigitalME and doing this kind of work for clients.

chunks.heading: Automation targets: social media, email marketing and PPC
chunks.text: Ross names the three areas where businesses most often get stuck: social media strategy, email marketing and PPC (pay-per-click advertising). He argues that automating these channels is what lets a company keep trading during and after a disruption like a pandemic. He also says the goal is to be ready to "trade and serve your customers whether there's a second wave of Covid19 or not."

chunks.heading: Worked example: a gym moving its services online
chunks.text:
Ross uses a gym as the model case and notes the same logic applies to dance, cooking or language classes. When gyms closed, many members cancelled, were afraid to return, or adjusted to training at home. The gyms that adapted followed this sequence:

1. Moved services online, with group and one-to-one workout sessions.
2. Created an irresistible free lead magnet (his example: a "dream abs at home" freebie) and pushed it across social media.
3. Used that freebie to build an email list quickly.
4. Used the list to pre-sell meal plans and 30-day fat-burn packages.
5. Put the content into a membership site, so revenue keeps coming in "in their sleep."

The pattern is: free lead magnet, social distribution, email list, pre-sold digital products, then a membership site that runs automatically.

chunks.heading: Knowing how is not the same as making it work
chunks.text: Ross says the automation steps themselves are not hard to understand. The difficulty is making the system reliably produce quality leads 24/7. He states that "there's a massive difference between knowing how to do something and making it work."

chunks.heading: Why not to DIY the tooling
chunks.text: Ross reports that clients repeatedly tell him they wish they had come to him earlier instead of trying to work out CRM platforms, ActiveCampaign and Infusionsoft on their own. His advice is to get expert help with the CRM and email automation stack rather than teaching yourself the tools while the business is under pressure.

chunks.heading: DigitalME's agency model
chunks.text: Ross started DigitalME to reshape the B2C and B2B markets. The agency has a team of experts involved through the whole process of taking a company online and getting it ready to trade and serve customers. The offer is end-to-end implementation (strategy, CRM, email automation and ads) rather than courses or advice alone. He contrasts this with the small business owners who bought a "how to create a webpage in 5 simple steps" course, got no leads, and asked for refunds.
